la:verb:sentio.gloss: to feel, to sense, to perceive (with the senses)
senses: to feel, to sense, to perceive (with the senses)
to perceive, be aware of, to be sensible of, to notice mentally, to understand (by using one's senses)
to have an opinion or opine, to think, feel, judge, suppose
la:verb:sentio.html:
sentĭo, si, sum, 4 (
perf. sync. sensti, ), v. a.
Physically.
In gen., to discern by the senses; to feel, hear, see, etc.; to perceive, be sensible of (syn. percipio).
With acc.: calorem et frigus,; cf.: duritiem saxi,; sq.: feram nare sagaci (venaticā), Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 346 Vahl.): varios rerum odores,: sucum in ore,: suavitatem cibi,: varios rerum colores,: sonitum,: nil aegri,: utrumque (calorem et frigus) manu,: famem,: morbos articularios,.—In mal. part.: sensit delphina Melantho,.—Pass.: posse prius ad angustias veniri, quam sentirentur,before they should be observed,.—
With inf. or an, object-clause: sei movero me seu secari sensero,: sentio aperiri fores. : nec quisquam moriens sentire videtur, Ire foras animam,: sentire sonare, Munro.—
Absol.: perpetuo quoniam sentimus,; ; : qui (homines) corruant, sed ita, ut ne vicini quidem sentiant,.—
Of things: pupula cum sentire colorem dicitur album, —Absol.: haud igitur aures per se possunt sentire,: si quis corpus sentire refutat,; ; cf. ; .—
In partic.
To perceive the effects (esp. the ill effects) of any thing; to feel, experience, suffer, undergo, endure: sentiet, qui vir siem,: jam curabo sentiat, Quos attentarit,: quid ipse ad Avaricum sensisset, etc.,; cf. : Centupirini etiam ceterarum civitatum damna ac detrimenta senserunt,; ; cf. : tecum Philippos et celerem fugam Sensi,: (Apollinem) vindicem,: caecos motus orientis austri,: contracta aequora (pisces),: prima arma nostra (Salyi),: sentire paulatim belli mala,: famem,; : damnum,: cladem belli,: inopiam rerum omnium,; . 7, 6: incommoda belli,: lassitudo jam et sitis sentiebatur,: ubi primum dolorem aliquis sentit,; cf. : cujus ulceris dolorem sentire etiam spectantes videntur,: corporis aegri vitia sentire,: qui in urbe se commoverit ... sentiet, in hac urbe esse consules vigilantes, esse egregios magistratus, etc.,; cf. ; .—Absol.: iste tuus ipse sentiet Posterius,.—Of beasts, etc.: oves penuriam sentiunt,: frigus aut aestum,: praegelidam hiemem omnes pisces sentiunt,.—
Of things, to be affected or influenced by: meae istuc scapulae sentiunt,; : transitum exercitus (ager),: pestilentem Africum (Fecunda vitis),: lacus et mare amorem Festinantis eri,: alnos fluvii cavatas,; cf. : carbunculi cum ipsi non sentiant ignes,: eadem (gemma) sola nobilium limam sentit,is affected by,: cum amnis sentit aestatem, et ad minimum deductus est,: miramur quod accessionem fluminum maria non sentiant,: illa primum saxa auctum fluminis sentiunt, : totum mare sentit exortum ejus sideris,: caseus vetustatem,: herba cariem,: ferrum robiginem,. —
In the elder Pliny, to be susceptible of, to be subject or liable to a disease: morbos,: rabiem,: cariem,.—
Mentally.
Lit., to feel, perceive, observe, notice (syn. intellego).
With acc.: id jam pridem sensi et subolet mihi,; so, quid,: quando Aesculapi ita sentio sententiam,I observe, understand,: primus sentio mala nostra,: numquam illum ne minimā quidem re offendi, quod quidem senserim,that I have perceived,: ut cui bene quid processerit, multum illum providisse, cui secus, nihil sensisse dicamus,: praesentia numina sentit,; cf. ; et saep.: de victoriā atque exitu rerum sentire,: omnia me illa sentire quae dicerem, nec tantum sentire, sed amare,: illum sensisse quae scripsit,.—Poet.: ut vestram sentirent aequora curam,: nec inania Tartara sentit,i. e. does not die,.—
With inf. or an obj.-clause: quoniam sentio errare (eum),: hoc vir excellenti providentiā sensit ac vidit, non esse, etc.,: suspicionem populi sensit moveri,: quod quid cogitent, me scire sentiunt, etc.,: postquam nihil esse pericli Sensimus,: non nisi oppressae senserunt (civitates), etc.,.—
With rel.- or interrog.-clause: scio ego et sentio ipse, quid agam,: jam dudum equidem sentio, suspicio Quae te sollicitet,: quoniam sentio, Quae res gereretur,: si quid est in me ingenii, quod sentio quam sit exiguum,: ex quo fonte hauriam, sentio,: victrices catervae Sensere, quid mens rite, quid indoles ... Posset,.—With the indic., in a rel.clause: sentio, quam rem agitis,.—
With de: hostes postea quam de profectione eorum senserunt,became aware of their retreat,; .—(ε) With nom. of part. (poet.): sensit terrae sola maculans,: sensit medios delapsus in hostis,.—(ζ) Absol.: vehementer mihi est irata: sentio atque intellego,; cf. ; : mentes sapientium cum e corpore excessissent sentire ac vigere (opp. carere sensu),; cf. : (Aristoteles) paeana probat eoque ait uti omnes, sed ipsos non sentire cum utantur,; cf. : priusquam hostes sentirent,; ; .— Impers. pass.: non ut dictum est, in eo genere intellegitur, sed ut sensum est,.—
To feel, experience (with acc. of the feeling; rare): quidquid est quod sensum habet, id necesse est sentiat et voluptatem et dolorem,: tenesne memoriā quantum senseris gaudium, cum, etc.,: non sentire amisso amico dolorem,; 121, 7: victoriae tantae gaudium sentire,; cf.: segnius homines bona quam mala sentire,.—
Transf. (in consequence of mental perception), to think, deem, judge, opine, imagine, suppose (syn.: opinor, arbitror): si ita sensit, ut loquitur, est homo impurus,; cf.: jocansne an ita sentiens,; : fleri potest, ut recte quis sentiat, et id quod sentit, polite eloqui non possit,: humiliter demisseque sentire,: tecum aperte, quod sentio, loquar,; cf.: quod sentio scribere,: causa est haec sola, in quā omnes sentirent unum atque idem,: idemque et unum sentire,: sapiens de dis immortalibus sine ullo metu vera sentit,.—With acc. and inf.: idem, quod ego, sentit, te esse huic rei caput,; cf.: nos quidem hoc sentimus: si, etc. ... non esse cunctandum,: voluptatem hanc esse sentiunt omnes,,

3, 6 Madv. ad loc.: sensit in omni disputatione id fieri oportere,; 5, 8, 23; ; ; : sic decerno, sic sentio, sic affirmo, nullam rerum publicarum conferendam esse cum eā, quam, etc.,.—With two acc. (very rare): aliquem bonum civem, (cf. , supra, where Orell. omits esse).—With de and abl.: cum de illo genere rei publicae quae sentio dixero,; so, quid de re publicā,; 1, 38, 60: quid de quo,: quid gravius de vobis,; ; cf.: qui omnia de re publicā praeclara atque egregia sentirent,were full of the most noble and generous sentiments,: mirabiliter de te et loquuntur et sentiunt,: male de illo,: sentire cum aliquo, to agree with one in opinion: tecum sentio,; : cum Caesare sentire,; ; cf.: nae iste haud mecum sentit,: ab aliquo sentire, to dissent from, disagree with: abs te seorsum sentio,judge otherwise, think differently,: ut abs te seorsus sentiam De uxoriā re, Afran. ap. P.: Gr. Omnia istaec facile patior, dum hic hinc a me sentiat. Tr. Atqui nunc abs te stat, is on my side, (cf. ab); cf. also: qui aliunde stet semper, aliunde sentiat,.—

In partic., publicists' and jurid. t. t., to give one's opinion concerning any thing; to vote, declare, decide (syn. censeo): sedens iis assensi, qui mihi lenissime sentire visi sunt,; ; : quae vult Hortensius omnia dicat et sentiat,: si judices pro causā meā senserint,decided in my favor,; cf.: in illam partem ite quā sentitis, Vet. Form. ap. .—Hence, sensa, ōrum, n. (acc. to II. B.).
Thoughts, notions, ideas, conceptions (class. but very rare): sententiam veteres, quod animo sensissent, vocaverunt ... Non raro tamen et sic locuti sunt, ut sensa sua dicerent: nam sensus corporis videbantur, etc.,: exprimere dicendo sensa,: sensa mentis et consilia verbis explicare,.—
Opinions, doctrines (late Lat.): sensa et inventa Disarii,.

la:noun:sensus.gloss: faculty or power of perceiving; perception, feeling, sensation, sense
senses: faculty or power of perceiving; perception, feeling, sensation, sense
la:noun:sensus.html:
sensus, ūs, m.
sentio
,
the faculty or power of perceiving, perception, feeling, sensation, sense, etc.
Corporeal, perception, feeling, sensation: omne animal sensus habet: sentit igitur et calida et frigida et dulcia et amara, nec potest ullo sensu jucunda accipere et non accipere contraria: si igitur voluptatis sensum capit, doloris etiam capit. etc.,: moriendi sensum celeritas abstulit,: si quis est sensus in morte,: (Niobe) posuit sensum saxea facta mali,: sensum voluptatemque percipere,.

—

A sense, capacity for feeling: ut idem interitus sit animorum et corporum nec ullus sensus maneat, etc.,: tactus corporis est sensus,: oculorum,; so, oculorum, aurium,; ; ; cf. videndi,: audiendi,: quod neque oculis neque auribus neque ullo sensu percipi potest,: quamquam oriretur (tertia philosophiae pars) a sensibus, tamen non esse judicium veritatis in sensibus,: res subjectae sensibus,: gustatus, qui est sensus ex omnibus maxime voluptarius,: sensus autem interpretes ac nuntii rerum in capite et facti et conlocati sunt,: omne animal sensus habet,: carent conchae visu, omnique sensu alio quam cibi et periculi,: ab eā parte opus orsus, ut a sensu ejus, averteret,.—
Mental, feeling, sentiment, emotion, affection; sense, understanding, capacity; humor, inclination, disposition, frame of mind, etc.: ipse in commovendis judicibus eis ipsis sensibus, ad quos illos adducere vellem, permoverer,: an vos quoque hic innocentium cruciatus pari sensu doloris adficit?: vestri sensus ignarus,: humanitatis,; : applicatio animi cum quodam sensu amandi ... ut facile earum (bestiarum) sensus appareat ... sensus amoris exsistit, etc.,; cf.: ipsi intellegamus naturā gigni sensum diligendi,: meus me sensus, quanta vis fraterni sit amoris, admonet,: utere argumento ipse sensus tui,: nihil est tam molle, tam aut fragile aut flexibile quam voluntas erga nos sensusque civium,: quae mihi indigna et intolerabilia videntur, ea pro me ipso et animi mei sensu ac dolore pronuntio,.—
Opinion, thought, sense, view: animi,: valde mihi placebat sensus ejus de re publicā,: (orator) ita peragrat per animos hominum, ita sensus mentesque pertractat, ut, etc.,: qui est iste tuus sensus, quae cogitatio? Brutos ut non probes, Antonios probes?: dissidenti sensus suos aperire,: sensus reconditi,.—
Esp., the common feelings of humanity, the moral sense, taste, discretion, tact in intercourse with men, often called in full sensus communis (sometimes with hominum), and often in other phrases of similar force: ut in ceteris (artium studiis) id maxime excellat, quod longissime sit ab imperitorum intellegentiā sensuque disjunctum, in dicendo autem vitium vel maximum sit a volgari genere orationis atque a consuetudine communis sensus abhorrere,: quae versantur in sensu hominum communi,; : communis ille sensus in aliis fortasse latuit,; : sit in beneficio sensus communis,; ; ; : rarus sensus communis in illā fortunā,. —Plur., : ea sunt in communibus infixa sensibus,; so, vulgaris popularisque sensus,: haec oratio longe a nostris sensibus abhorrebat,; cf.: mirari solebam istum in his ipsis rebus aliquem sensum habere, quem scirem nullā in re quicquam simile hominis habere,.—
Transf. (in the poets, and also in prose after the Aug. per.), of the thinking faculty, sense, understanding, mind, reason (syn.: mens, ratio).
In gen. (rare): misero quod omnes Eripit sensus mihi,; cf.: tibi sensibus ereptis mens excidit,; ; : (quibus fortuna) sensum communem abstulit,common sense, (in another signif., v.supra, II. A. fin., and infra, 2. fin.): eam personam, quae furore detenta est, quia sensum non habet, etc.,: nec potest animal injuriam fecisse, quod sensu caret,.—
In partic., of discourse.
Abstr., sense, idea, notion, meaning, signification (syn.: sententia, notio, significatio, vis; poet. and post-Aug.; freq. in Quint.): nec testamenti potuit sensus colligi, : verba, quibus voces sensusque notarent,: is verbi sensus,: quae verbis aperta occultos sensus habent,: ambiguitas, quae turbare potest sensum,: verba duos sensus significantia,: ἀλληγορία aliud verbis, aliud sensu ostendit, : Pomponium sensibus celebrem, verbis rudem,: horum versuum sensus atque ordo sic, opinor, est,: egregie dicta circa eumdem sensum tria,.—Introducing a quotation: erat autem litterarum sensus hujusmodi,.—With gen. person: salvo modo poëtae sensu,the meaning,.—
Concr., a thought expressed in words, a sentence, period (postAug.): sensus omnis habet suum finem, poscitque naturale intervallum, quo a sequentis initio dividatur,; ; cf. : puer ut sciat, ubi claudatur sensus,: ridendi, qui velut leges prooemiis omnibus dederunt, ut intra quattuor sensus terminarentur,: verbo sensum cludere multo optimum est, et saep.—Hence, communes sensus (corresp. with loci), commonplaces, .

la:noun:senatus.gloss: alternative letter-case form of Senātus (“the Roman Senate”)
senses: alternative letter-case form of Senātus (“the Roman Senate”)
senate, a council of elders, parliament, or similar deliberative body
la:noun:senatus.html:
sĕnātus, ūs (
gen. senati, ; ; Sisenn. ap. ; ; also cited ap. P.; ; ; . acc. to ; P.; Don. ; P.; id. Fragm. ap. Don. ; also , acc. to the pr. man. of the Cod. Medic.; cf. .—Another form of the gen. senatuis, C. Fann. ap. P.; Sisenn. ap. ; also, as it seems,, yet the passage itself is wanting.—In old orthog. SENATVOS, S. C. de Bacch.; dat. senato, ), m.
senex; like γερουσία from γέρων; cf. ;
, the council of the elders, the Senate, the supreme council in Rome, concerning whose origin, constitution, powers, etc., v. senator; cf. Momms. Hist. of Rome, 1, 113 sqq.; 1, 406 sqq. Am. ed.; Becker, Antiq. 2, 1, p. 339 sq.; 2, 2, p. 385 sq.; 2, 3, p. 210 sq.; and the authors there cited: quae (consilium, ratio, sententia) nisi essent in senibus, non summum consilium majores nostri appellassent senatum. Apud Lacedaemonios quidem ii, qui amplissimum magistratum gerunt, ut sunt sic etiam nominantur senes,: Romuli senatus, qui constabat ex optimatibus,: (Majores nostri) senatum rei publicae custodem collo caverunt,: senatus rem pu blicam tenuit, ut pleraque senatūs auctori tate gererentur,: ut potentia senatus atque auctoritas minueretur,: cum potestas in populo, auctoritas in senatu sit,: nec per senatum solvi hac lege possumus,.—Freq. in the phrase: senatus populusque Romanus (often written S. P. Q. R.), the Senate and people of Rome, i.e. the State, the republic, ; ; very rarely in reverse order: populus et senatus Romanus,: populi Romani senatusque verbis,; ; Vitr. praef. 1, 1: senatus (senati, senatuis, v.supra) consultum, a decree of the Senate (v. consulo, P. a. III.); senatūs auctoritas, the same (v. auctoritas, 4.): censuit senatus, the Senate resolved; v. censeo, 3. b. (cf. also decerno, I. A., and decretum, s. v. decerno fin.): senatum convocare,; : senatus

est continuo convocatus frequensque convenit, ; cf.: senatus frequens vocatu Drusi in curiam venit,: vocare senatum,: cito cogere,; ; : habere senatum,; ; : agere,; : eo die non fuit senatus neque postero,no session of the Senate,, a, 1: eodem die Tyriis (legatis) est senatus datus frequens,i. e. gave audience,; so, dare senatum (legatis),; ; et saep.: senatu dimisso,: dimittere senatum,: mittere,: multa ejus (Catonis) et in senatu et in foro vel provisa prudenter vel acta constanter ferebantur,in the meetings of the Senate,; cf.: (Catilina) etiam in senatum venit,: ad senatum adduci, in senatu poni, id. Fragm. ap. : ad senatum in Capitolio stare,: in senatu sedere, to sit among the senators, on the senatorial seats (in the theatre), ; cf.: in orchestram senatumque descendit,: in senatum venire,to become a senator,: de senatu cooptando,nominating, electing,; : de senatu movere,: senatu movere, Dietsch; and: senatu emovere,: ex or de senatu eicere,; ; ; ; ; (v. 1. lego and eicio): seminarium senatus, i. e. the order of Knights, from which new senators were elected, .—Also of the Senate of other nations: senatus (Gaditanus), Asin. ap. : Aeduorum,: Venetorum,fin. et saep.: Judaeorum,.—

Trop., a council, i. e. consultation (mostly ante-class.): de re argentariā senatum convocare in corde consiliarium,: sibi senatum consili in cor convocare,; ; : deūm,.

la:noun:sententia.gloss: a way of thinking, view, opinion, judgement or sentence
senses: a way of thinking, view, opinion, judgement or sentence
a purpose, intention, will (one's thinking in respect to the future)
a vote of opinion (expressed in senate in response to an interrogātiō)
an authoritative decision, pronouncement, judgement, decree
a thought expressed in words; a sense, meaning, signification
la:noun:sententia.html:
sententĭa, ae, f.
for sentientia, from sentio
,
a way of thinking, opinion, judgment, sentiment; a purpose, determination, decision, will, etc.
Lit. (cf.: opinio, voluntas, studium).
In gen.: quoniam sententiae atque opinionis meae voluistis esse participes, nihil occultabo et quoad potero, vobis exponam, quid de quāque re sentiam,: sententia et opinio mea,: senis sententia de nuptiis,: de aliquā re,; ; cf.: de diis immortalibus habere non errantem et vagam, sed stabilem certamque sententiam,: de hac sententiā Non demovebor,; cf. : de sententiā deducere, deicere, depellere, deterrere, decedere, desistere, etc., v. h. vv.: nisi quid tua secus sententia est,; cf.: mihi sententia eadem est,: adhuc in hac sum sententiā, nihil ut faciamus nisi, etc.,: eā omnes stant sententiā,; cf.: perstat in sententiā Saturius,; so, in sententiā manere, permanere, etc., v. h. vv.: non prima sed melior vicit sententia,.—Plur.: variis dictis sententiis, quarum pars censebant, etc.,: erant sententiae, quae censerent,: sententiae numerantur, non ponderantur,: nos quibus Cotta tantum modo locos ac sententias hujus disputationis tradidisset,the leading thoughts,.—Prov.: quot homines, tot sententiae,many men, many minds,; . —
In the phrases,
Sententia est, with subj.-clause, it is my purpose, will, opinion, etc., : si honestatem tueri ac retinere sententia est,if one's purpose be, if one be determined,; and: stat sententia, with obj.clause, ; cf., parenthetically: sic stat sententia,.—
De sententiā alicujus aliquid facere, : neque ego haud committam, ut si quid peccatum siet, Fecisse dicas de meā sententiā,according to my wish, to suit me,: gerere,; cf. ; , C, § 11; 7, 5 fin.; et saep.—
Meā quidem sententiā, in my opinion or judgment, as I think: nimis stulte faciunt, meā quidem sententiā,: meā quidem sententiā,; ; ; ; ; and simply meā sententiā,; ; ; ; —
Ex meā (tuā, etc.) sententiā, according to my (thy, etc.) wish: quoniam haec evenerunt nostrā ex sententiā,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; and more freq., simply ex sententiā, to one's mind or liking, , 1, 18; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep. (v. also infra, B. 2.).—(ε) Praeter animi sententiam, against one's inclination: quam (crapulam) potavi praeter animi mei sententiam,.—
In partic., publicists' and jurid. t.t., an official determination, a decision, sentence, judgment, vote (cf. suffragium): SENATVOS SENTENTIAM VTEI SCIENTES ESETIS, EORVM SENTENTIA ITA FVIT, S. C. de Bacch.: (L. Tarquinius) antiquos patres majorum gentium appellavit, quos priores sententiam rogabat,: non viribus ... res magnae geruntur, sed consilio, auctoritate, sententiā,: (Marcellinus) sententiam dixit, ut, etc. ... postea Racilius de privatis me primum sententiam rogavit, etc.,: accurate sententiam dixi ... factum est senatusconsultum in meam sententiam,: DE SENATVOS SENTENTIAD ... DE PR. VRBANI SENATVOSQVE SENTENTIAD, S. C. de Bacch.: ex senatus sententiā,: victos paucis sententiis,.—Hence, sententiam dare, to vote: meae partes exquirendae magis sententiae quam dandae sunt,: omnes in eam sententiam ierunt,: cum in hanc sententiam pedibus omnes issent,: aliquem sequor, aliquem jubebo sententiam dividere,to divide the question,; cf.: quod fieri in senatu solet ... cum censuit aliquis quod ex parte mihi placeat, jubeo illum dividere sententiam et sequor,.—Hence, de eventu fortuna judicat, cui de me sententiam non do, I give no vote, .—Of the people in the comitia: de singulis magistratibus sententiam ferre,: de quo foedere populus Romanus sententiam non tulit,.—Of the votes of judges: itur in consilium: servus ille innocens omnibus sententiis absolvitur, quo facilius vos hunc omnibus sententiis condemnare possitis,; : condemnatur enim perpaucis sententiis,: M. Cato (judex) sententiam dixit, pronounced the decision or sentence, : sententiis paribus reus absolvitur,.—
Ex animi mei (tui) sententiā, in the formula of an oath, to the best of my (your) knowledge and belief, on my (your) conscience: (majores) jurare ex sui animi sententiā quemque voluerunt,: quod ex animi tui sententiā juraris, id non facere perjurium est,; ; fin.—In a play on this signif. and that of ex sententiā, supra: ridicule illud L. Nasica censori Catoni, cum ille: Ex tui animi sententiā tu uxorem habes? Non hercule, inquit, ex animi mei sententiā,; cf. ; sqq.— Transf., as a formula of assurance: me quidem, ex animi mei sententiā, nulla oratio laedere potest,by my faith,.—
Transf., of words, discourse, etc., sense, meaning, signification, idea, notion, etc.: sonitum ut possis sentire, neque illam Internoscere, verborum sententiam quae sit,: cum verbum potest in duas plurisve sententias accipi,: cum continenter verbum non in eādem sententiā ponitur,: formantur et verba et sententiae paene innumerabiliter,: cognitā sententiā verba subtiliter exquiri noluerunt,: quod summum bonum a Stoicis dicitur convenienter naturae vivere, id habet hanc, ut opinor, sententiam: cum virtute congruere semper,: haec (philosophia) nos docuit, ut nosmet ipsos nosceremus: cujus praecepti tanta vis, tanta sententia est, ut ea non homini cuipiam, sed Delphico deo tribueretur,such depth of meaning,: legis (with vis),: de Domitio dixit versum Graecum eādem sententiā, quā etiam nos habemus Latinum: Pereant amici, etc.,: est vitium in sententiā, si quid absurdum, aut alienum est,; cf. .—
Concr.
In gen., a thought expressed in words; a sentence, period: dum de singulis sententiis breviter

disputo, : est brevitate opus, ut currat sententia, etc.,: initia et clausulae sententiarum,; cf. ; ; ; 9, 4, 18; 9, 4, 29; 10, 1, 130 al.—

In partic., a philosophical proposition, an aphorism, apophthegm, maxim, axiom (cf. praeceptum): selectae (Epicuri) brevesque sententiae, quas appellatis κυρίας δόξας, : quid est tam jucundum cognitu atque auditu, quam sapientibus sententiis gravibusque verbis ornata oratio et perpolita,: acutae,: concinnae acutaeque,; ; ; ; 11, 3, 120 al.: (Sophocles) sententiis densus,; cf. ; : subiti ictūs sententiarum,.

tos senes, etc. ... ut petulantia magis est adulescentium quam senum ... sic ista senilis stultitia senum levium est ... Appius et caecus et senex, etc. ... senem, in quo est adulescentis aliquid, probo, etc., : senem in patriam revertentem, unde puer profectus sum (the words of Hannibal, who was not yet fifty years of age),: mixta senum ac juvenum densentur funera,; cf.: haec recinunt juvenes dictata senesque,: aeque neglectum pueris senibusque nocebit,: ter aevo functus senex,i. e. Anchises),; so, = senex,; ; ; 12, 182; 12, 540; ; ; : (Servius Tullius) seniores a junioribus divisit,; cf. of the same: C. Tubero in Historiarum primo scripsit, Servium Tullium ... eos (milites) ab anno septimo decimo ad annum quadragesimum sextum juniores, supraque eum annum seniores appellasse,: centuriae juniorum seniorumque,.—Poet.: centuriae seniorum simply, for seniores,: curae fuit consulibus et senioribus Patrum, ut, etc.,: consulares ac seniores (opp. juniores Patrum),: omnium seniorum, matrum familiae, virginum precibus et fletu excitati,: sapienter, ut senior, suaserat,: juniores a senioribus consilium petiverunt,: haec ... laeti audiere juvenes, ingrata senioribus erant,: hinc inter juniores senesque orta contentio est,.—In eccl. Lat., an elder in the synagogue or church, ; Johan. 1.

senses: senator (a member of the Roman Senate)
la:noun:senator.html:
sĕnātor, ōris, m.
senex
,
a senator, a member of the Roman Senate, a body consisting originally of one hundred eminent citizens, selected by Romulus for their age, wisdom, and experience, out of the noblest families, to be his council in the government. When the Sabines were incorporated with Rome, the number was doubled; and Tarquin the Elder raised it to three hundred; Sulla to four hundred; Julius Cæsar to nine hundred, while Augustus reduced it to six hundred. Originally, patricians alone were eligible to seats in the Senate; but later additions were made from the Knights (v. senatus). The senators were nominated by the kings; and, after they were expelled, by the consuls and dictators. Later, the censors revised the roll of senators every lustrum, excluding members regarded as unworthy. (On the powers of the Senate, the privileges, dress, etc., of its members, v. Dict. of Antiq. s. v. Senatus.) —Sing.: huic (senatori) jussa tria sunt: ut assit, etc.,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; —Plur., ; ; —Out of Rome, of the Nervii, .—Of the Rhodians, .—Of the Macedonians ( = σὐνεδροι), et saep.— Of the Persians,.

la:verb:senesco.html:
sĕnesco, nŭi, 3 (
gerundive: senescendi homines, Müll. N. cr.), v. inch. n. [seneo], to grow old, become aged; to grow hoary.
Lit. (rare): ita sensim aetas senescit,; cf.: tempora labuntur tacitisque senescimus annis,: senescente jam Graeciā,: solve senescentem mature equum,: arbores senescunt,: Solon significat se cottidie aliquid addiscentem senescere. .—In perf.: avus (Augusti) tranquillissime senuit,: ego senui et progressioris aetatis sum,.—In gerundive: longissimum spatium senescendorum hominum id (seclum) putarant, Müll. N. cr.—
Transf.
For the usual consenescere, to grow old or gray in an occupation, etc., i. e. to linger too long over it: inani circa voces studio senescunt,.—
(Causa pro effectu.) To decay or diminish in strength; to grow weak, feeble, or powerless; to waste away, fall off, wane, decline, etc. (the prevailing signif. of the word in prose and poetry; cf. consenesco; while inveterasco is to grow better by age).
Of living subjects (a favorite expression of Livy; perh. not in Cic., but cf. consenesco, II. 2.): Hannibalem jam et famā senescere et viribus,; cf. of the same,: otio senescere,: non esse cum aegro senescendum,: dis hominibusque accusandis senescere,to pine away, Drak.; cf.: amore senescit habendi,: socordiā,; : ne (agni) desiderio senescant,.— Of doves,: quod antiquatur et senescit prope interitum est,.—
Of things: quaedam faciunda in agris potius crescente lunā quam senescente,in the waning of the moon,; so, luna (opp. crescens),; : arbores hiemali tempore cum lunā simul senescentes,: nunc pleno orbe, nunc senescente (al. senescentem) exiguo cornu fulgere lunam,: continuā messe senescit ager,becomes exhausted, worn out,: prata,: uniones, i. e. grow pale or dim, ; cf. smaragdi,: caseus in salem,grows salt with age,: coma, falls out, Domit. ap. : monumenta virūm, decay (with delapsa), et saep.: mensis senescens,drawing to an end, closing, Müll.; so, hiems,.—Of abstr. things: oratorum laus senescit,; cf.: ut laus senescens,: senescere civitatem otio,: omnia orta occidunt et aucta senescunt,; cf. Fabri ad ; so, somnia,: vires, Gerl.; : Hannibalis vis,: bellum,; : pugna,: fama,; ; cf. rumores,: consilia,: vitia (opp. maturescente virtute),: invidia,: fortuna (opp. florere),: amor,.
